scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Meaning 'to wander' or 'drift', this style replaced sacred drums with the melodic harmony of guitars and ukuleles to tell stories of the post-1800s world.
This is Hula ʻauana. 19th–20th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (sw51ThkIvRM)
Title card: Hula ʻauana · USA (Hawaii) · 19th–20th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Hula ʻauana developed in the 19th and 20th centuries as Hawaiian culture adapted to Western influences, specifically Christian morality and melodic harmony.

While hula was once banned or suppressed following the American overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom and the 1896 ban on the Hawaiian language in schools, a cultural resurgence in the late 1960s revitalized the practice.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Hula ʻauana is performed to comment on significant people, places, or events, or to express emotions.
While it can be performed for entertainment at festivals like the Merrie Monarch (established 1971), it remains a vital method of preserving the Hawaiian language and oral history.
The concept of 'mana' (spiritual power) remains central to the poetry (mele), and performers are taught that they bear the consequences of the poetry they deliver.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance dramatizes the words of a mele (song) through complex hand motions and a library of basic foot and hip movements.
Hand gestures represent nature, such as waves or trees, or emotions like sadness.
Basic steps include the kāholo (side-to-side), kaʻo (swaying hips), kāwelu, hela (pointing foot forward), ʻuwehe (lifting heels and pushing knees forward), and ʻami (hip rotations).

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Unlike ancient hula, ʻauana uses Western-influenced portable acoustic stringed instruments.
The primary ensemble includes the ʻukulele (rhythm or lead), the guitar (often played in 'slack key' or 'steel guitar' styles), and the double bass to maintain rhythm.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Regalia in hula ʻauana is generally less revealing than traditional styles, reflecting 19th-century Western influence.
Women often wear long dresses or skirts rather than the traditional topless pāʻū.
Dancers frequently wear lei in various forms: lei poʻo (headpieces), necklaces, and kupeʻe (bracelets or anklets).

scenes.title: The people
narration: The 'kumu hula' is the source of knowledge and master teacher of the dance.

In the 20th century, Western artists like Elvis Presley popularized a fusion of hula and rock in the film 'Blue Hawaii' with the song 'Rock A Hula Baby', though this is distinct from traditional practice.
While related dances like the Tahitian 'ote'a or Maori haka exist across Polynesia, hula is unique to the Hawaiian Islands.
Hula ʻauana is the direct descendant of hula kahiko (ancient hula).
